summary: Defines an experimental way to run SNMP over OSI transports, instead of over UDP. It is not a standard. It was replaced by RFC 1418.

eli5.summary: The device-checkup tool normally uses one kind of delivery. This shows how to use a different kind, the OSI one.

questions: how does snmp work over connectionless transport
why would snmp run over osi instead of udp
subtitle: An experimental approach to running the Simple Network Management Protocol over OSI transport layers instead of UDP.

tldr.problem: SNMP was designed to work with UDP as its transport layer, but some networks operate on OSI protocols rather than the Internet Protocol suite. Networks with OSI infrastructure and SNMP deployments needed a way to use SNMP over their native transport protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1161 defines mappings to run SNMP over two OSI transport services: CLTS (Connectionless-mode Transport Service, similar to UDP) and COTS (Connection-Oriented Transport Service, similar to TCP). The mappings are straightforward: SNMP messages are sent directly over CLTS, while COTS requires establishing a connection, sending one or more SNMP messages, then releasing the connection.
tldr.outcome: This experimental specification demonstrated that SNMP's design was transport-agnostic. However, the Internet standardized on UDP and later TCP, and OSI transports were not widely adopted. The specification was replaced by RFC 1418 with only minor changes.

today: RFC 1161 was replaced by RFC 1418, which made only minor corrections and retained experimental status. OSI transport protocols were not widely deployed in practice; the Internet community standardized on UDP for SNMP (and later TCP for secure variants). SNMP over OSI transports remains experimental and is not used in modern networks, though the RFC successfully proved SNMP's transport independence.

sections.title: Background and Motivation
sections.content:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) was originally designed to operate over UDP (User Datagram Protocol) as defined in RFC 1157. However, SNMP's design was intentionally transport-independent, allowing it to function over any reliable or unreliable datagram service. As OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) protocols gained adoption in some networks, organizations operating both TCP/IP infrastructure and OSI infrastructure wanted to manage OSI-based equipment using their existing SNMP investments and tools.

RFC 1161 provides the mappings necessary to run SNMP over OSI transport services. OSI defines two transport services: CLTS (Connectionless-mode Transport Service), which is similar to UDP in that it sends individual packets without a connection; and COTS (Connection-Oriented Transport Service), which is similar to TCP in that it requires establishing and closing connections. The mappings are straightforward because SNMP itself handles reliability and sequencing at the application layer; the transport layer is simply a delivery mechanism.
sections.eli5: SNMP is a way to check on network devices and computers. Different networks use different delivery systems. This explains how to use SNMP with the OSI delivery system, which some networks used instead of the Internet system.

sections.title: Mapping SNMP onto Connectionless Transport
sections.content:
Mapping SNMP to CLTS (the OSI connectionless transport service) is the simpler of the two approaches. The SNMP message is simply sent as-is over CLTS, with addressing based on OSI network service addresses (NSAPs). Unlike the Internet suite, which uses well-known ports (port 161 for SNMP, port 162 for traps), OSI uses transport selectors—opaque strings of bytes that the destination interprets to demultiplex incoming messages.

By convention, CLTS-based SNMP uses the four-byte ASCII string snmp as the transport selector for normal SNMP requests and replies, and the nine-byte ASCII string snmp-trap for trap messages. The addressing scheme is expressed using the string encoding defined in RFC 1278, for example: "snmp"/NS+4900590800200038bafe00, where NS+ indicates OSI network service and the hex string is the network address. This approach preserves SNMP's original datagram semantics: a manager sends a request and may or may not receive a response, and there is no connection state.
sections.eli5: SNMP messages go directly over OSI like postcards—no setup, no connection. Each postcard has a label that says 'snmp' so the receiving computer knows it's an SNMP message.

sections.title: Mapping SNMP onto Connection-Oriented Transport
sections.content:
Mapping SNMP to COTS is more complex because COTS requires establishing a connection before sending data. Unlike TCP-based SNMP (which is rarely used), the mapping for COTS does not assume that responses come on the same connection as requests. A manager may open a connection, send a request, and either wait for the response on that connection or receive it on a different connection. The responder, however, must send responses to requests on the same connection the request arrived on.

The initiator is responsible for releasing (closing) the connection, though the responder may close it due to resource constraints. The RFC recommends that connections remain open for an implementation-specific time, allowing multiple SNMP messages to be exchanged before closing to amortize the connection setup cost. However, SNMP retransmission, sequencing, and reliability are still managed by the SNMP application layer, not by the COTS service—SNMP is not assuming the connection guarantees delivery or ordering beyond what SNMP itself ensures.
sections.eli5: With OSI's connection-based delivery, you have to call up the other computer first, send your message, and then hang up. You can send multiple messages on one call before hanging up, but SNMP still handles making sure the message got there—the connection is just the delivery truck, not a guarantee.

sections.title: Addressing and Transport Selectors
sections.content:
OSI addressing differs fundamentally from the Internet model. The Internet uses IP addresses and ports; OSI uses NSAPs (Network Service Access Points) and selectors. For CLTS and COTS over CLNP (Connectionless Network Protocol), the SNMP transport selector is conventionally the four ASCII bytes snmp. For COTS over TP4/CLNP (TP4 being Transport Protocol Class 4), the same snmp selector is used. For COTS over TP0/X.25 (where X.25 is an older packet switching technology), SNMP uses a different scheme: X.25 protocol identifiers instead of selectors, with the protocol ID 03018200 for SNMP and 03019000 for traps.

RFC 1161 recommends that user interfaces to SNMP supporting multiple transport backings use a common addressing syntax from RFC 1278. For example, an address might be written as Internet=cheetah.nyser.net+161+2 for UDP or "snmp"/NS+4900590800200038bafe00 for OSI CLNP. This allows users to specify addresses in a consistent format regardless of the underlying transport, while tools can parse and map them to the appropriate mechanism.
sections.eli5: OSI uses different address labels than the Internet. Instead of a 'port number,' OSI uses a 'selector' which is just a name like 'snmp.' Different OSI transports use different kinds of addresses, but they can all be written in a standard format so programs can understand them.

sections.title: Design Rationale and Layering
sections.content:
An important design choice in RFC 1161 is placing SNMP at the OSI transport layer rather than at the application layer. The RFC argues that network management is fundamentally different from other applications: it is a function that sits between the operating system and user applications, providing visibility into network state. The RFC cites RFC 1052 (which develops this argument in full) to justify mapping SNMP to transport services rather than wrapping it in OSI application protocols.

This design choice preserves SNMP's lightweight character and allows a single SNMP implementation to work over multiple transport backings without requiring complex application-layer service interactions. It also means that SNMP can function independently of higher-layer OSI protocols, making it suitable for network management scenarios where the full OSI stack is not present or the stack itself is being diagnosed.
sections.eli5: The designers decided SNMP should sit at a lower level in OSI than most applications, so it can check on network equipment even when the network software is broken or only partially set up.
